claim: A truncated β-catenin protein of approximately 40 kDa was detected in Vav-Cre+ RK-Ctnnb1fl/fl bone marrow cells.
source: We previously obtained the Ctnnb1 exons 2–6 floxed model (Brault et al., 2001). We aimed to ablate β-catenin protein in all hematopoietic cells using Vav-Cre, but found accumulation of a truncated form of β-catenin protein of approximately 40 kDa in bone marrow (BM) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with a previous report (Jeannet et al., 2008).
evidence: Immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrates the presence of a truncated β-catenin protein in Vav-Cre+ RK-Ctnnb1fl/fl cells.

claim: Both Ctnnb1-targeted strains used in previous studies retain a truncated protein in hematopoietic cells.
source: One notable observation is that both Ctnnb1-targeted strains used in previous studies retain a truncated protein in hematopoietic cells (Jeannet et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jeannet et al., 2008.

claim: Deletion of exons 2–6 or exons 3–6 in both Ctnnb1-targeted models may have allowed in-frame translation from downstream exons, giving rise to an N-terminally truncated β-catenin protein of 40–50 kDa.
source: The Ctnnb1 gene has 15 exons, deletion of exons 2–6 or exons 3–6 in both models (Brault et al., 2001; Huelsken et al., 2000) may have allowed in-frame translation from downstream exons, giving rise to an N-terminally truncated β-catenin protein of 40–50 kDa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of the Ctnnb1 gene and the targeting strategy used in previous models, supported by citations.

claim: An N-terminally truncated form of β-catenin protein has longer half-life.
source: Because the N-terminus of β-catenin contains phosphorylation sites for ubiquitin-dependent degradation, an N-terminally truncated form of β-catenin protein has longer half-life, and its ectopic expression has been shown to stimulate proliferation and apoptosis of intestinal crypts (Wong et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wong et al., 1998 and draws from established knowledge about β-catenin regulation.

claim: A C-terminally truncated β-catenin is a naturally occurring β-catenin paralog in planarians and acts as a negative regulator of full-length β-catenin during planarian eye photoreceptor specification.
source: In addition, a C-terminally truncated β-catenin is a naturally occurring β-catenin paralog in planarians, and acts as a negative regulator of full-length β-catenin during planarian eye photoreceptor specification (Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Su et al., 2017.

claim: The new Ctnnb1 targeting strategy removes 13 of a total of 15 Ctnnb1 exons.
source: To achieve complete ablation of β-catenin protein, we re-targeted the Ctnnb1 gene locus by inserting LoxP sites into introns 1 and 14, respectively (Figure 1A) so that a Cre recombinase removes 13 of a total of 15 Ctnnb1 exons.
evidence: The targeting strategy is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The new targeting strategy can generate a true β-catenin null mutation without generating truncated form(s).
source: Lineage-negative BM cells and peripheral T cells from CreER+Ctnnb1fl/fl mice were cultured in vitro with tamoxifen or its carrier solvent, DMSO, and immunoblotting validated effective ablation of β-catenin protein without generating truncated form(s) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 1B demonstrates complete ablation of β-catenin without truncated forms.

claim: CreER+Ctnnb1fl/fl mice exhibited morbidity within 10 days when treated with tamoxifen in vivo for four consecutive days.
source: When the whole mice were treated with tamoxifen in vivo for four consecutive days, however, CreER+Ctnnb1fl/fl mice exhibited morbidity within 10 days, while CreER+Ctnnb1+/+ mice remained healthy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating ablating β-catenin in multiple organs may have severely compromised vital functions.
evidence: Survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 demonstrates morbidity in CreER+Ctnnb1fl/fl mice.

claim: Treatment of BM chimera recipients with tamoxifen did not cause lethality.
source: After ≥6 weeks when the BM chimeras were stably established, treatment of the recipients with the same tamoxifen regimen did not cause lethality (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Effective ablation of β-catenin was observed in sorted CD45.2+CreER+Ctnnb1fl/fl thymocytes, splenic T cells, and total BM cells from tamoxifen-treated BM chimeras.
source: Effective ablation of β-catenin was observed in sorted CD45.2+CreER+Ctnnb1fl/fl thymocytes, splenic T cells, and total BM cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 1D demonstrates effective ablation of β-catenin in multiple cell types.

claim: PCR products from F1 and R1 primers were barely detectable in sorted CD45.2+ BM cells from tamoxifen-treated CreER+Ctnnb1fl/fl recipients.
source: We further determined the efficacy of deleting floxed exons in genomic DNAs, where the PCR products from F1 and R1 primers were detected from the WT Ctnnb1 allele (Figure 1A), but were barely detectable in sorted CD45.2+ BM cells from tamoxifen-treated CreER+Ctnnb1fl/fl recipients (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Quantitative PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A demonstrates deletion efficiency at the genomic DNA level.

claim: Effective deletion of Ctnnb1 transcripts was validated by RT-PCR using primer 13F in combination with primer 15R.
source: Effective deletion of Ctnnb1 transcripts was also validated by RT-PCR using primer 13F (complementary to the deleted exon 13) in combination with primer 15R (complementary to undeleted exon 15) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: RT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B demonstrates deletion efficiency at the transcript level.

claim: Jup transcripts were only one fiftieth as abundant as Ctnnb1 transcripts in WT cells.
source: On the mRNA level, Jup transcripts were only one fiftieth as abundant as Ctnnb1 transcripts in WT cells, but both Jup and Ctnnb1 transcripts were effectively deleted in tamoxifen-treated CreER+Ctnnb1fl/flJupfl/fl BM cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: RT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C demonstrates relative abundance of Jup and Ctnnb1 transcripts.

claim: γ-catenin protein was readily detectable in WT hepatocytes and was greatly diminished in hepatocytes in tamoxifen-treated CreER+Ctnnb1fl/flJupfl/fl mice.
source: Consistent with low Jup transcript abundance, detection of γ-catenin protein in WT or targeted BM cells proved to be challenging; however, γ-catenin protein was readily detectable in WT hepatocytes and was greatly diminished in hepatocytes in tamoxifen-treated CreER+Ctnnb1fl/flJupfl/fl mice (non-BM chimeras, Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D demonstrates effective ablation of γ-catenin in hepatocytes.

claim: Total thymic cellularity was similar in WT chimeras and those lacking β-catenin alone or both β-catenin and γ-catenin.
source: Following tamoxifen-induced target gene deletion in the chimeras, total thymic cellularity was similar in WT chimeras and those lacking β-catenin alone or both β-catenin and γ-catenin (Figure 1E).
evidence: Thymic cellularity data in Figure 1E shows no significant differences among genotypes.

claim: Each thymic subset (DN, DP, CD4+, CD8+) was detected at similar frequency among all genotypes examined.
source: Thymocyte maturation follows sequential stages from CD4–CD8–double negative (DN) to CD4+CD8+double positive (DP) followed by further differentiation to CD4+ or CD8+ single positive cells. Each thymic subset was detected at similar frequency among all genotypes examined (Figure 1F).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 1F shows similar frequencies of thymic subsets among genotypes.

claim: DN and DP cells exhibited more active proliferation than CD4+ and CD8+ thymocytes.
source: By intracellular staining of Ki67, DN and DP cells exhibited more active proliferation than CD4+ and CD8+ thymocytes, and each subset showed similar frequency of Ki67+ cells among all genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Ki67 staining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A demonstrates proliferation rates in different thymic subsets.

claim: Each thymic subset showed similar frequency of Ki67+ cells among all genotypes.
source: By intracellular staining of Ki67, DN and DP cells exhibited more active proliferation than CD4+ and CD8+ thymocytes, and each subset showed similar frequency of Ki67+ cells among all genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Ki67 staining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A shows no significant differences in proliferation among genotypes.

claim: DN thymocytes showed modestly increased susceptibility to apoptosis than thymocytes in later stages.
source: Detection of active Caspase-3/7 revealed that DN thymocytes showed modestly increased susceptibility to apoptosis than thymocytes in later stages, and each subset showed similar frequency of Caspase-3/7+ cells among all genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Caspase-3/7 staining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B demonstrates apoptosis rates in different thymic subsets.

claim: Each thymic subset showed similar frequency of Caspase-3/7+ cells among all genotypes.
source: Detection of active Caspase-3/7 revealed that DN thymocytes showed modestly increased susceptibility to apoptosis than thymocytes in later stages, and each subset showed similar frequency of Caspase-3/7+ cells among all genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Caspase-3/7 staining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B shows no significant differences in apoptosis among genotypes.

claim: Distribution of DN1-4 subsets was similar among all genotypes.
source: In addition, subfractionating the DN thymocytes based on CD25 and CD44 expression showed that distribution of DN1-4 subsets was similar among all genotypes (Figure 1G).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 1G shows similar distribution of DN subsets among genotypes.

claim: None of the CreER+ WT and CreER+Ctnnb1fl/flJupfl/fl BM chimeras showed signs of malignant transformation of thymocytes or other hematopoietic lineage cells during 16 weeks of monitoring after tamoxifen treatment.
source: A cohort of CreER+ WT and CreER+Ctnnb1fl/flJupfl/fl BM chimeras (n = 5 each) was monitored for 16 weeks after tamoxifen treatment, and none of these mice showed signs of malignant transformation of thymocytes or other hematopoietic lineage cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from long-term monitoring of the mice.

claim: Complete loss of β-catenin or both β- and γ-catenin did not detectably cause T cell developmental blocks, or alterations in thymocyte proliferative capacity or survival.
source: These analyses showed that complete loss of β-catenin or both β- and γ-catenin did not detectably cause T cell developmental blocks, or alterations in thymocyte proliferative capacity or survival.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figures 1E-G and Figure 1—figure supplements 5A-B.

claim: Activated CD4+ T cells predominantly differentiate into CXCR5–SLAMhi T helper 1 (TH1) and CXCR5+SLAMloT follicular helper (TFH) lineage cells in response to acute viral infections.
source: In response to acute viral infections, antigen-specific mature CD4+ and CD8+ T cells mount protective immune responses by clonal expansion and differentiation into functional effector cells. To test the requirements for β-catenin and γ-catenin in mature T cell responses, we infected tamoxifen-treated BM chimera with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus Armstrong strain (LCMV-Arm) to elicit acute viral infection. Activated CD4+ T cells predominantly differentiate into CXCR5–SLAMhi T helper 1 (TH1) and CXCR5+SLAMloT follicular helper (TFH) lineage cells (Crotty, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Crotty, 2014 and represents established knowledge.

claim: TFH cells depend on Tcf1 and Lef1 for Bcl6 induction and further differentiation.
source: TFH cells depend on Tcf1 and Lef1 for Bcl6 induction and further differentiation (Choi et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015.

claim: Deletion of β-catenin alone or in combination with γ-catenin did not affect the frequency of TH1 or TFH cells at the peak response (8 days post-infection).
source: TFH cells depend on Tcf1 and Lef1 for Bcl6 induction and further differentiation (Choi et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015); in contrast, deletion of β-catenin alone or in combination with γ-catenin did not affect the frequency of TH1 or TFH cells at the peak response (i.e., 8 days post-infection, dpi) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 2A shows similar frequencies of TH1 and TFH cells among genotypes at 8 dpi.

claim: Bcl6-expressing germinal center (GC)-TFH cells were detected at similar frequency among all genotypes at 8 days post-infection.
source: In addition, Bcl6-expressing germinal center (GC)-TFH cells were detected at similar frequency among all genotypes (Figure 2B), suggesting that β-catenin and γ-catenin are not essential for TFH cell differentiation.
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 2B shows similar frequencies of GC-TFH cells among genotypes.

claim: β-catenin and γ-catenin are not essential for TFH cell differentiation.
source: In addition, Bcl6-expressing germinal center (GC)-TFH cells were detected at similar frequency among all genotypes (Figure 2B), suggesting that β-catenin and γ-catenin are not essential for TFH cell differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing similar frequencies of GC-TFH cells among genotypes.

claim: Fully differentiated cytotoxic effector CD8+T cells downregulate Tcf1.
source: Whereas TFH cells maintain Tcf1 expression similar to naïve CD4+ T cells (Gullicksrud et al., 2017), fully differentiated cytotoxic effector CD8+T cells downregulate Tcf1 (Gullicksrud et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gullicksrud et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2010.

claim: Loss of Tcf1 has little impact on differentiation of effector CD8+T cells.
source: Consistent with this Tcf1 expression pattern, loss of Tcf1 has little impact on differentiation of effector CD8+T cells (Shan et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shan et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2010.

claim: Deletion of β-catenin alone or both β/γ-catenin did not detectably affect generation of antigen-specific effector CD8+T cells.
source: Not surprisingly, deletion of β-catenin alone or both β/γ-catenin did not detectably affect generation of antigen-specific effector CD8+T cells, identified as IFN-γ-producing cells upon stimulation with peptides derived from the LCMV glycoprotein (GP) 33 epitope (Figure 2C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 2C shows similar frequencies of IFN-γ-producing CD8+ T cells among genotypes.

claim: GP33-specific effector CD8+T cells showed similar capacity of producing TNF-α and similar expression of granzyme B among all genotypes.
source: The GP33-specfic effector CD8+T cells showed similar capacity of producing TNF-α and similar expression of granzyme B among all genotypes (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that β-catenin and γ-catenin are dispensable for CD8+ T cells to differentiate into functional cytotoxic T cells.
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figures 2C and 2D show similar TNF-α production and granzyme B expression among genotypes.

claim: β-catenin and γ-catenin are dispensable for CD8+ T cells to differentiate into functional cytotoxic T cells.
source: The GP33-specfic effector CD8+T cells showed similar capacity of producing TNF-α and similar expression of granzyme B among all genotypes (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that β-catenin and γ-catenin are dispensable for CD8+ T cells to differentiate into functional cytotoxic T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing similar functional capacity of effector CD8+ T cells among genotypes.

claim: Tcf1 long isoform ablation led to profound reduction of memory TH1 and TFH cells.
source: Tcf1 is expressed in long and short isoforms with the former having the capacity of interacting with β-catenin through its N-terminal domain (Staal et al., 2008; Xue and Zhao, 2012). Previously we ablated the Tcf1 long isoform, which led to profound reduction of memory TH1 and TFH cells (Gullicksrud et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gullicksrud et al., 2017.

claim: Tcf1 is required for memory CD8+ T cells.
source: Tcf1 is also required for memory CD8+ T cells (Jeannet et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jeannet et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2010.

claim: CXCR5+ memory TFH cells were detected at similar frequency in WT and β/γ-catenin-null BM chimeras at ≥40 days post-infection.
source: To determine if β-catenin and γ-catenin are required for memory T cells, we analyzed the infected BM chimeras at ≥40 dpi. During 15–16 and 30–31 dpi, we added two rounds of tamoxifen treatment to the LCMV-infected BM chimeras, so as to prevent rebound of undeleted cells and ensure persistent deletion of β/γ-catenin proteins. CXCR5+ memory TFH cells were detected at similar frequency in WT and β/γ-catenin-null BM chimeras (Figure 2E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 2E shows similar frequencies of memory TFH cells among genotypes.

claim: GP33-specific memory CD8+ T cells were not diminished in β/γ-catenin-null BM chimeras and preserved similar capacity of producing TNF-α.
source: GP33-specific memory CD8+ T cells were not diminished in β/γ-catenin-null BM chimeras and preserved similar capacity of producing TNF-α (Figure 2F).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 2F shows similar frequencies and function of memory CD8+ T cells among genotypes.

claim: Loss of β-catenin and γ-catenin did not detectably affect T cell responses at either effector or memory phase.
source: Collectively, loss of β-catenin and γ-catenin did not detectably affect T cell responses at either effector or memory phase.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: β-catenin ablation using previously Ctnnb1-targeted models did not show potent impact on maintenance of HSCs.
source: β-catenin ablation using previously Ctnnb1-targeted models did not show potent impact on maintenance of HSCs (Ruiz-Herguido et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ruiz-Herguido et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2007.

claim: Null mutation of β-catenin alone or both β/γ-catenin did not affect BM cellularity.
source: Consistent with these observations, null mutation of β-catenin alone or both β/γ-catenin did not affect BM cellularity (Figure 3A), or the frequency of Lin–Sca1+c-Kit+ (LSK) cells, in which HSCs were enriched (Figure 3B).
evidence: Data in Figure 3A shows similar BM cellularity among genotypes.

claim: Null mutation of β-catenin alone or both β/γ-catenin did not affect the frequency of Lin–Sca1+c-Kit+ (LSK) cells.
source: Consistent with these observations, null mutation of β-catenin alone or both β/γ-catenin did not affect BM cellularity (Figure 3A), or the frequency of Lin–Sca1+c-Kit+ (LSK) cells, in which HSCs were enriched (Figure 3B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 3B shows similar frequencies of LSK cells among genotypes.

claim: HSCs with long-term repopulation capacity, as marked by CD150+CD48– phenotype, were detected at similar frequency among all genotypes.
source: HSCs with long-term repopulation capacity, as marked by CD150+CD48– phenotype, were detected at similar frequency among all genotypes (Figure 3B), suggesting that loss of β/γ-catenin did not perturb HSC homeostasis.
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 3B shows similar frequencies of HSCs among genotypes.

claim: Loss of β/γ-catenin did not perturb HSC homeostasis.
source: HSCs with long-term repopulation capacity, as marked by CD150+CD48– phenotype, were detected at similar frequency among all genotypes (Figure 3B), suggesting that loss of β/γ-catenin did not perturb HSC homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing similar frequencies of HSCs among genotypes.

claim: AML LSCs have been reported to critically depend on β-catenin using the MLL-AF9 or MLL-ENL mouse models.
source: Unlike HSCs, AML LSCs have been reported to critically depend on β-catenin using the MLL-AF9 or MLL-ENL mouse models (Wang et al., 2010; Yeung et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2010; Yeung et al., 2010.

claim: Complete deletion of β-catenin in AML cells was achieved as determined by immunoblotting of sorted CD45.2+GFP+Mac1+ BM cells from primary recipients on day 28 after BM transplantation.
source: The efficacy of this regimen was validated by immunoblotting for β-catenin in CD45.2+GFP+Mac1+ AML cells in the BM of 1o recipients (Figure 3D).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 3D demonstrates complete deletion of β-catenin in AML cells.

claim: Primary recipients of WT and β-catenin-deficient AML cells showed similar rate of survival.
source: The 1o recipients in both groups showed similar rate of survival (Figure 3E), suggesting that β-catenin null mutation did not affect the onset of AML.
evidence: Survival data in Figure 3E shows no significant difference between groups.

claim: β-catenin null mutation did not affect the onset of AML.
source: The 1o recipients in both groups showed similar rate of survival (Figure 3E), suggesting that β-catenin null mutation did not affect the onset of AML.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar survival rates of primary recipients.

claim: Both WT and β-catenin-deficient AML LSCs showed similar capacity of propagating AML as determined by longitudinal tracking of CD45.2+Mac1+ GFP+ AML leukemia burden in peripheral blood cells.
source: To specifically investigate self-renewal of AML LSCs, we sort-purified CD45.2+GFP+Lin–Mac1loc-Kithi Sca1loCD16/CD32hi cells as AML LSCs from the 1o recipients (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for gating strategy), followed by transplantation into secondary (2o) recipients (Figure 3C). Both WT and β-catenin-deficient AML LSCs showed similar capacity of propagating AML as determined by longitudinal tracking of CD45.2+Mac1+ GFP+ AML leukemia burden in peripheral blood cells (PBCs, Figure 3F), and by the survival rate of 2o recipients (Figure 3E).
evidence: Data in Figure 3F shows similar leukemia burden in secondary recipients of WT and β-catenin-deficient LSCs.

claim: Secondary recipients of WT and β-catenin-deficient AML LSCs showed similar survival rate.
source: Both WT and β-catenin-deficient AML LSCs showed similar capacity of propagating AML as determined by longitudinal tracking of CD45.2+Mac1+ GFP+ AML leukemia burden in peripheral blood cells (PBCs, Figure 3F), and by the survival rate of 2o recipients (Figure 3E).
evidence: Survival data in Figure 3E shows no significant difference between groups.

claim: Secondary recipients of β/γ-catenin-deficient AML LSCs showed similar survival as those of WT or β-catenin-deficient LSCs.
source: In an independent experiment, 2o recipients of β/γ-catenin-deficient AML LSCs showed similar survival as those of WT or β-catenin-deficient LSCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Survival data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows no significant difference among groups.

claim: The data collectively argue against an essential role of β-catenin for AML LSCs.
source: These data collectively argue against an essential role of β-catenin for AML LSCs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the AML LSC transplantation data.

claim: There are four members in the Tcf/Lef family: Tcf1, Lef1, Tcf3 and Tcf4 (encoded by Tcf7, Lef1, Tcf7l1, and Tcf7l2, respectively).
source: To further substantiate the unexpected lack of impact on AML LSCs by null mutation of β/γ-catenin, we extended our AML studies to determine a requirement for Tcf/Lef family TFs that interact with β-catenin. There are four members in the Tcf/Lef family: Tcf1, Lef1, Tcf3 and Tcf4 (encoded by Tcf7, Lef1, Tcf7l1, and Tcf7l2, respectively).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Tcf/Lef family.

claim: Tcf1 and Lef1 proteins were ablated in thymocytes of CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO mice as determined by intracellular staining.
source: Following treatment with the same tamoxifen regimen as above, the CreER+Tcf-qKO mice did not exhibit early lethality, and Tcf1 and Lef1 proteins were ablated in thymocytes of CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO mice as determined by intracellular staining (Figure 4B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4B demonstrates ablation of Tcf1 and Lef1 proteins.

claim: Ablation of Tcf4 protein was effective in thymocytes as determined by immunoblotting.
source: While ablation of Tcf4 protein was also effective in thymocytes as determined by immunoblotting (Figure 4B), Tcf3 protein was not reliably detected in thymocytes or BM cells (not shown), likely due to its expression in very low abundance (see Figure 4C).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 4B demonstrates ablation of Tcf4 protein.

claim: Tcf3 protein was not reliably detected in thymocytes or BM cells, likely due to its expression in very low abundance.
source: While ablation of Tcf4 protein was also effective in thymocytes as determined by immunoblotting (Figure 4B), Tcf3 protein was not reliably detected in thymocytes or BM cells (not shown), likely due to its expression in very low abundance (see Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, with reference to Figure 4C showing low transcript abundance.

claim: Deletion efficacy for Tcf3 protein was independently verified in mouse embryonic fibroblasts using the same ES clone.
source: It should be noted that deletion efficacy for Tcf3 protein was independently verified in mouse embryonic fibroblasts in a recent report using the same ES clone (Mašek et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mašek et al., 2016.

claim: The targeted exon in Tcf7l1 transcripts was as effectively deleted as that in Tcf7l2 transcripts, in spite of the low abundance.
source: We further verified with quantitative RT-PCR that the targeted exon in Tcf7l1 transcripts was as effectively deleted as that in Tcf7l2 transcripts, in spite of the low abundance (Figure 4C).
evidence: RT-PCR data in Figure 4C demonstrates deletion efficiency of Tcf7l1 and Tcf7l2 transcripts.

claim: Tamoxifen treatment resulted in >90% reduction in thymic cellularity in CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and CreER+Tcf-qKO mice.
source: Tamoxifen treatment resulted in >90% reduction in thymic cellularity in CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and CreER+Tcf-qKO mice, but did not detectably affect CreER+Tcf3/4-dKO thymocyte numbers (Figure 4D).
evidence: Data in Figure 4D shows profound reduction in thymic cellularity in Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and Tcf-qKO mice.

claim: Tamoxifen treatment did not detectably affect CreER+Tcf3/4-dKO thymocyte numbers.
source: Tamoxifen treatment resulted in >90% reduction in thymic cellularity in CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and CreER+Tcf-qKO mice, but did not detectably affect CreER+Tcf3/4-dKO thymocyte numbers (Figure 4D).
evidence: Data in Figure 4D shows no significant change in thymic cellularity in Tcf3/4-dKO mice.

claim: Tcf1 is required for DP thymocyte survival.
source: Consistent with a requirement for Tcf1 for DP thymocyte survival (Ioannidis et al., 2001), tamoxifen-treated CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and CreER+Tcf-qKO mice showed profound reduction in DP thymocyte frequency, with concomitant relative increase in CD4+ and CD8+ single positive thymocyte frequency (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ioannidis et al., 2001.

claim: Tamoxifen-treated CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and CreER+Tcf-qKO mice showed profound reduction in DP thymocyte frequency, with concomitant relative increase in CD4+ and CD8+ single positive thymocyte frequency.
source: Consistent with a requirement for Tcf1 for DP thymocyte survival (Ioannidis et al., 2001), tamoxifen-treated CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and CreER+Tcf-qKO mice showed profound reduction in DP thymocyte frequency, with concomitant relative increase in CD4+ and CD8+ single positive thymocyte frequency (Figure 4E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4E shows altered thymic subset distribution in Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and Tcf-qKO mice.

claim: CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and CreER+Tcf-qKO mice both showed DN1 accumulation and apparent loss of DN2 thymocytes.
source: Within the DN compartment, CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and CreER+Tcf-qKO mice both showed DN1 accumulation and apparent loss of DN2 thymocytes (Figure 4F), in line with a key function of Tcf1 in specification of early thymic progenitors to T cell lineage (Germar et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2011).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4F shows altered DN subset distribution in Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and Tcf-qKO mice.

claim: Tcf1 has a key function in specification of early thymic progenitors to T cell lineage.
source: Within the DN compartment, CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and CreER+Tcf-qKO mice both showed DN1 accumulation and apparent loss of DN2 thymocytes (Figure 4F), in line with a key function of Tcf1 in specification of early thymic progenitors to T cell lineage (Germar et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Germar et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2011.

claim: CreER+Tcf3/4-dKO mice exhibited little or modest changes in thymic development.
source: In all these critical aspects, CreER+Tcf3/4-dKO mice exhibited little or modest changes; furthermore, the defects observed in CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO mice were not detectably more exacerbated in CreER+Tcf-qKO mice with additional deletion of Tcf3 and Tcf4.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data in Figures 4D-F.

claim: The defects observed in CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO mice were not detectably more exacerbated in CreER+Tcf-qKO mice with additional deletion of Tcf3 and Tcf4.
source: In all these critical aspects, CreER+Tcf3/4-dKO mice exhibited little or modest changes; furthermore, the defects observed in CreER+Tcf1/Lef1-dKO mice were not detectably more exacerbated in CreER+Tcf-qKO mice with additional deletion of Tcf3 and Tcf4.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data in Figures 4D-F.

claim: Tcf3 and Tcf4 are not essential for thymopoiesis.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that Tcf3 and Tcf4 are not essential for thymopoiesis and further validate critical function of Tcf1 and Lef1 among the Tcf/Lef family in T cell development.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of severe defects in Tcf3/4-dKO mice and the lack of exacerbation in Tcf-qKO compared to Tcf1/Lef1-dKO mice.

claim: Tcf1 and Lef1 have critical function among the Tcf/Lef family in T cell development.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that Tcf3 and Tcf4 are not essential for thymopoiesis and further validate critical function of Tcf1 and Lef1 among the Tcf/Lef family in T cell development.
evidence: This is inferred from the severe defects observed in Tcf1/Lef1-dKO and Tcf-qKO mice.

claim: Primary recipients of MLL-AF9-infected Tcf-qKO BM cells showed similar survival rate as those of WT BM cells.
source: Given the demonstrated efficacy of ablating Tcf/Lef factors in hematopoietic cells, we extended our studies to investigate their requirement in AML LSCs. We used Lin– BM cells from tamoxifen-treated CreER+ WT or CreER+Tcf-qKO mice directly for the AML studies, without establishing BM chimeras. The 1o recipients of MLL-AF9-infected Tcf-qKO BM cells showed similar survival rate as those of WT BM cells (Figure 4G), indicating ablation of all four Tcf/Lef TFs did not affect AML onset.
evidence: Survival data in Figure 4G shows no significant difference between groups.

claim: Ablation of all four Tcf/Lef TFs did not affect AML onset.
source: The 1o recipients of MLL-AF9-infected Tcf-qKO BM cells showed similar survival rate as those of WT BM cells (Figure 4G), indicating ablation of all four Tcf/Lef TFs did not affect AML onset.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar survival rates of primary recipients.

claim: WT and Tcf-qKO AML LSCs isolated from primary recipients showed similar capacity of propagating AML leukemic cells in PBCs in secondary recipients.
source: In addition, WT and Tcf-qKO AML LSCs isolated from the 1o recipients showed similar capacity of propagating AML leukemic cells in PBCs in 2o recipients (Figure 4H), resulting in similar survival rate of the 2o recipients (Figure 4G).
evidence: Data in Figure 4H shows similar leukemia burden in secondary recipients of WT and Tcf-qKO LSCs.

claim: Secondary recipients of WT and Tcf-qKO AML LSCs showed similar survival rate.
source: In addition, WT and Tcf-qKO AML LSCs isolated from the 1o recipients showed similar capacity of propagating AML leukemic cells in PBCs in 2o recipients (Figure 4H), resulting in similar survival rate of the 2o recipients (Figure 4G).
evidence: Survival data in Figure 4G shows no significant difference between groups.

claim: The data do not support an essential requirement for Tcf/Lef and β-catenin proteins in AML LSCs.
source: Collectively, our data do not support an essential requirement for Tcf/Lef and β-catenin proteins in AML LSCs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the AML LSC data with Tcf-qKO cells.

claim: Constitutive activation of non-canonical NF-κB pathway impairs AML LSC self-renewal.
source: It is of note that the lack of impact on AML LSCs by ablating Tcf/Lef TFs or β-catenin was not due to technical issues, because we have used the same protocol to demonstrate that 1) constitutive activation of non-canonical NF-κB pathway (Xiu et al., 2018) or 2) genetic ablation of Groucho/TLE corepressors (to be described elsewhere) impairs AML LSC self-renewal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xiu et al., 2018.

claim: Genetic ablation of Groucho/TLE corepressors impairs AML LSC self-renewal.
source: It is of note that the lack of impact on AML LSCs by ablating Tcf/Lef TFs or β-catenin was not due to technical issues, because we have used the same protocol to demonstrate that 1) constitutive activation of non-canonical NF-κB pathway (Xiu et al., 2018) or 2) genetic ablation of Groucho/TLE corepressors (to be described elsewhere) impairs AML LSC self-renewal.
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data to be described elsewhere.

claim: β-catenin and γ-catenin are not essential for thymocyte development.
source: By use of the newly established β-catenin null mutation, this study clarifies on a long-standing controversy and provides more conclusive evidence indicating that β-catenin and γ-catenin are not essential for thymocyte development, T cell responses to viral infection at either effector or memory phase.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the thymocyte development data presented.

claim: β-catenin and γ-catenin are not essential for T cell responses to viral infection at either effector or memory phase.
source: By use of the newly established β-catenin null mutation, this study clarifies on a long-standing controversy and provides more conclusive evidence indicating that β-catenin and γ-catenin are not essential for thymocyte development, T cell responses to viral infection at either effector or memory phase.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the T cell response data presented.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal domain in Tcf1, which abrogates interaction with β-catenin, does reduce thymic cellularity and compromise TFH cell differentiation at effector and memory phases.
source: This is in stark contrast to the versatile functions described for Tcf1 and Lef1 in T lineage cells (Raghu et al., 2019). We previously showed that deletion of the N-terminal domain in Tcf1, which abrogates interaction with β-catenin, does reduce thymic cellularity and compromise TFH cell differentiation at effector and memory phases (Gullicksrud et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gullicksrud et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2017.

claim: Tcf1 may engage coactivators other than β-catenin to exert biological functions.
source: Given the apparent lack of impact upon β/γ-catenin deletion, Tcf1 may engage coactivators other than β-catenin to exert those biological functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between effects of Tcf1 N-terminal deletion and β-catenin deletion.

claim: Tcf1 interacts with a Ser21-phosphorylated form of Ezh2 to cooperatively induce Bcl6 and Icos during TFH cell differentiation in response to acute viral infection.
source: Indeed, we recently reported that Tcf1 interacts with a Ser21-phosphorylated form of Ezh2 to cooperatively induce Bcl6 and Icos during TFH cell differentiation in response to acute viral infection (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: Genetic alterations in Wnt-β-catenin pathway components are not among the primary driver mutations of AML.
source: Although genetic alterations in Wnt-β-catenin pathway components are not among the primary driver mutations of AML (Papaemmanuil et al., 2016; Tyner et al., 2018), frequent translocation products including MLL-AF9 result in elevated β-catenin accumulation (Lane et al., 2011; Müller-Tidow et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Papaemmanuil et al., 2016; Tyner et al., 2018.

claim: Frequent translocation products including MLL-AF9 result in elevated β-catenin accumulation.
source: Although genetic alterations in Wnt-β-catenin pathway components are not among the primary driver mutations of AML (Papaemmanuil et al., 2016; Tyner et al., 2018), frequent translocation products including MLL-AF9 result in elevated β-catenin accumulation (Lane et al., 2011; Müller-Tidow et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lane et al., 2011; Müller-Tidow et al., 2004.

claim: The reported requirements for β-catenin in AML LSCs using previously Ctnnb1-targeted mouse strains may be likely ascribed to unwanted effects by the truncated β-catenin protein.
source: It is surprising that ablation of neither β-catenin nor Tcf/Lef TFs affected LSC self-renewal in the AML mouse model. The reported requirements for β-catenin using previously Ctnnb1-targeted mouse strains may be likely ascribed to unwanted effects by the truncated β-catenin protein.
evidence: This is speculation based on the discrepancy between current findings and previous reports.

claim: For the purpose of eradicating AML LSCs, targeting β-catenin may not be as effective as previously hoped.
source: Our data do not refute the facts that aberrant activation of β-catenin has pathological effects, and there is no denial of therapeutic values in inhibiting Wnt-β-catenin pathway for debulking AML blasts. The findings in this study nonetheless caution that for the purpose of eradicating AML LSCs, targeting β-catenin may not be as effective as previously hoped.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing lack of effect of β-catenin deletion on AML LSCs.

claim: β-catenin is a transcriptional coregulator that interacts with transcription factors in the Tcf/Lef family to modulate gene expression.
source: β-catenin is a known transcriptional coregulator that interacts with transcription factors in the Tcf/Lef family and others to modulate gene expression (Cadigan, 2012; Mosimann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Cadigan, 2012; Mosimann et al., 2009.

claim: Phosphorylation at a cluster of Ser/Thr residues in the N-terminus of β-catenin results in proteasome-mediated degradation of β-catenin.
source: β-catenin protein is regulated through post-translational modifications. Phosphorylation at a cluster of Ser/Thr residues in its N-terminus results in proteasome-mediated degradation of β-catenin (Cadigan, 2012; Mosimann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Cadigan, 2012; Mosimann et al., 2009.

claim: Activation of Wnt and prostaglandin E2 signaling pathways leads to inactivation of the kinases responsible for β-catenin phosphorylation and therefore accumulation of β-catenin protein.
source: Activation of several signaling pathways such as Wnt and prostaglandin E2 leads to inactivation of the kinases that are responsible for β-catenin phosphorylation and therefore accumulation of β-catenin protein (Goessling et al., 2011; Klaus and Birchmeier, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Goessling et al., 2011; Klaus and Birchmeier, 2008.

claim: Aberrant β-catenin activation is frequently associated with malignant transformation and various cancers.
source: Due to its strong impact on transcription, the activity of β-catenin is tightly controlled, with aberrant β-catenin activation frequently associated with malignant transformation and various cancers (Clevers and Nusse, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Clevers and Nusse, 2012.

claim: Modest activation of β-catenin extends survival of thymocytes.
source: In the hematopoietic system, modest activation of β-catenin has been shown to have beneficial effects, such as extending survival of thymocytes (Xie et al., 2005) and regulatory T cells (Ding et al., 2008), promoting expansion of memory CD8+ T cells (Gattinoni et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2005.

claim: Modest activation of β-catenin extends survival of regulatory T cells.
source: In the hematopoietic system, modest activation of β-catenin has been shown to have beneficial effects, such as extending survival of thymocytes (Xie et al., 2005) and regulatory T cells (Ding et al., 2008), promoting expansion of memory CD8+ T cells (Gattinoni et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ding et al., 2008.

claim: Modest activation of β-catenin promotes expansion of memory CD8+ T cells.
source: In the hematopoietic system, modest activation of β-catenin has been shown to have beneficial effects, such as extending survival of thymocytes (Xie et al., 2005) and regulatory T cells (Ding et al., 2008), promoting expansion of memory CD8+ T cells (Gattinoni et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gattinoni et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2010.

claim: Excessive β-catenin activation through deletion of exon 3 of Ctnnb1 gene has detrimental effects on the function of hematopoietic stem cells.
source: However, excessive β-catenin activation, through deletion of exon 3 of Ctnnb1 gene (which encodes the Ser/Thr cluster in β-catenin protein), has detrimental effects on the function of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) (Kirstetter et al., 2006; Scheller et al., 2006), blocks thymocyte maturation and promotes thymocyte transformation (Guo et al., 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kirstetter et al., 2006; Scheller et al., 2006.

claim: Excessive β-catenin activation blocks thymocyte maturation and promotes thymocyte transformation.
source: However, excessive β-catenin activation, through deletion of exon 3 of Ctnnb1 gene (which encodes the Ser/Thr cluster in β-catenin protein), has detrimental effects on the function of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) (Kirstetter et al., 2006; Scheller et al., 2006), blocks thymocyte maturation and promotes thymocyte transformation (Guo et al., 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2007b.

claim: Genetic deletion of exons 3–6 of the Ctnnb1 gene caused modest developmental blocks and modest reduction in thymic cellularity during thymocyte maturation.
source: During thymocyte maturation, for example, genetic deletion of exons 3–6 of the Ctnnb1 gene caused modest developmental blocks and modest reduction in thymic cellularity (Xu et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2003.

claim: No thymocyte maturation defects were observed when Ctnnb1 exons 2–6 were inducibly deleted with Mx1-Cre.
source: In other reports, however, no thymocyte maturation defects were observed when Ctnnb1 exons 2–6 were inducibly deleted with Mx1-Cre (Cobas et al., 2004), or in chimeric mice reconstituted with fetal liver cells lacking β-catenin and its homologue, γ-catenin (Jeannet et al., 2008; Koch et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cobas et al., 2004.

claim: No thymocyte maturation defects were observed in chimeric mice reconstituted with fetal liver cells lacking β-catenin and γ-catenin.
source: In other reports, however, no thymocyte maturation defects were observed when Ctnnb1 exons 2–6 were inducibly deleted with Mx1-Cre (Cobas et al., 2004), or in chimeric mice reconstituted with fetal liver cells lacking β-catenin and its homologue, γ-catenin (Jeannet et al., 2008; Koch et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jeannet et al., 2008; Koch et al., 2008.

claim: Mature CD8+ T cells in β-catenin-targeted models showed intact response to viral infections.
source: Additionally, mature CD8+ T cells in these β-catenin-targeted models showed intact response to viral infections (Driessens et al., 2010; Prlic and Bevan, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Driessens et al., 2010; Prlic and Bevan, 2011.

claim: Tcf1 and Lef1 are expressed in T lineage cells among the Tcf/Lef family transcription factors.
source: On the other hand, among the Tcf/Lef family transcription factors (TFs) that interact with β-catenin, Tcf1 and Lef1 are expressed in T lineage cells (Staal et al., 2008; Xue and Zhao, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Staal et al., 2008; Xue and Zhao, 2012.

claim: Null mutations of Tcf1 alone or together with Lef1 show more profound T cell developmental blocks and more severe decrease in thymic cellularity than β-catenin deletion.
source: Null mutations of Tcf1 alone or together with Lef1 show more profound T cell developmental blocks and more severe decrease in thymic cellularity (Germar et al., 2011; Okamura et al., 1998; Verbeek et al., 1995; Weber et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Germar et al., 2011; Okamura et al., 1998; Verbeek et al., 1995; Weber et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2012b.

claim: Tcf1 has multifaceted roles in mature T cell responses including differentiation of follicular helper T cells.
source: Recent studies also revealed multifaceted roles of Tcf1 in mature T cell responses including differentiation of follicular helper T cells (Choi et al., 2015; Raghu et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2015; Raghu et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015.

claim: The presence of the truncated β-catenin protein in previously β-catenin-targeted models may functionally compensate for loss of full-length β-catenin, underlying the lack of severe defects in T cell development or mature T cell responses.
source: Therefore, the presence of the truncated β-catenin protein in previously β-catenin-targeted models may functionally compensate for loss of full-length β-catenin, underlying the lack of severe defects in T cell development or mature T cell responses.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of truncated β-catenin in previous models.

claim: The truncated β-catenin protein may function as a dominant negative.
source: On the other hand, the truncated β-catenin protein may function as a dominant negative, and this possibility then raises questions on observed requirements for β-catenin using the existing β-catenin-targeted models.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential function of truncated β-catenin.

claim: β-catenin is considered essential for self-renewal of leukemic stem cells in both chronic and acute myeloid leukemia.
source: For example, β-catenin is considered essential for self-renewal of leukemic stem cells (LSCs) in both chronic and acute myeloid leukemia (CML and AML, respectively) (Hu et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2010; Yeung et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2010; Yeung et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2007.
